title: “FAITH CAN MOVE MOUNTAINS”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS NEVER MEANT YOU COULD CONTROL THE MOUNTAIN?
paragraphs: “FAITH CAN MOVE MOUNTAINS”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS NEVER MEANT YOU COULD CONTROL THE MOUNTAIN?
The dangerous difference between trusting God for the impossible and trying to use faith to make God obey us.
There is a kind of faith that looks powerful from a distance but quietly collapses when God says no.
It knows how to declare.
It knows how to rebuke.
It knows how to speak confidently about breakthroughs.
It knows how to quote, “Faith can move mountains.”
But then the diagnosis remains.
The marriage still breaks.
The person you prayed for still dies.
The door stays closed.
The child does not come home.
The money does not suddenly appear.
The depression of circumstances does not lift overnight.
And somewhere in the silence, a terrible question begins whispering:
Was my faith not strong enough?
Maybe you have asked it.
Maybe someone made you ask it.

Maybe you prayed until your throat hurt. Maybe you fasted. Maybe you believed with everything you knew how to believe. Maybe you repeated the promises you had been taught to repeat, rebuked doubt whenever it surfaced, and waited for the mountain to move.
But it didn't.
And what wounded you most was not merely that the mountain remained.
It was the suspicion that God remained because you had failed Him.
Listen carefully.
What if the problem was never that your faith was too small?
What if the problem was that someone taught you to measure faith by how much control it gives you over outcomes?
Because Jesus never handed His disciples a spiritual remote control for reality.
He gave them something infinitely better.
He gave them Himself.
And understanding that may completely change the way you read one of His most famous sayings.
Jesus said:
“Ἐὰν ἔχητε πίστιν ὡς κόκκον σινάπεως…”
Ean echēte pistin hōs kokkon sinapeōs…
“If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed…”
Then He said that they could tell a mountain to move and it would move, concluding:
“καὶ οὐδὲν ἀδυνατήσει ὑμῖν.”
“…and nothing will be impossible for you.”
That is Matthew 17:20.
Those words are breathtaking.
But they become dangerous when ripped from their biblical setting and turned into a slogan meaning, “If I believe hard enough, God must produce the outcome I demand.”
That is not biblical faith.
That is an attempt to put sovereignty in human hands.
And God is still God.

The Greek word translated “faith” is πίστις — pistis. In the New Testament, its semantic range includes faith, belief, trust, faithfulness, and confidence. Biblical faith is not primarily mental force exerted upon reality.
It is trust directed toward God.
That distinction changes everything.
Jesus was not teaching His followers to have faith in faith.
He was teaching them to trust God.
And there is a universe of difference between those two things.
Faith in faith says:
“If I can believe strongly enough, I can make this happen.”
Faith in God says:
“I believe God is able—and even when I cannot command what He chooses, I can entrust myself completely to Him.”
One tries to control the mountain.
The other trusts the Lord who made it.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading this needs to stop pretending.
Because your mountain has not moved.
You have prayed about it for months.
Maybe years.
You watched other people testify about miracles while you quietly wondered why heaven seemed silent over your own life.
And somewhere along the way, disappointment started turning into shame.
Maybe God would have healed them if I had believed harder.
Maybe my marriage would have survived.
Maybe the business wouldn't have collapsed.
Maybe my child would have changed.
Maybe I ruined my miracle by doubting.
That burden can become spiritually devastating.
And it is not what Jesus intended His words to produce.
The context of Matthew 17 matters.

A desperate father had brought his suffering son to Jesus' disciples, but they could not heal him. Jesus subsequently delivered the boy. Later, the disciples privately asked Jesus why they had been unable to do it.
His response confronted their lack of faith.
Then came the mustard seed.
Then came the mountain.
In other words, Jesus' statement was born in the context of disciples discovering that spiritual power does not originate in themselves.
They were not sovereign.
God was.
And notice the shocking image Jesus chose.
A mustard seed.
Something tiny.
Jesus did not say:
“If your faith becomes enormous enough…”
He pointed toward something famously small.
That alone should disturb the popular idea that miracles happen because a Christian manufactures a sufficiently large quantity of psychological certainty.
The power is not located in the size of the believer.
The power belongs to God.
Tiny faith in an almighty God is not the same thing as enormous confidence in yourself.

The mountain-moving statement also fits a broader biblical world in which mountains can symbolize massive, seemingly immovable obstacles. The Hebrew Scriptures contain striking mountain imagery. Zechariah 4:7, for example, addresses an enormous obstacle before Zerubbabel:
“מִי־אַתָּה הַר־הַגָּדוֹל”
Mi-attah har-haggadol?
“Who are you, O great mountain?”
The mountain would become level before the work God had appointed.
Notice again who determined the mission.
God.
The mountain moved in service of God's purpose—not human ego.
This is where prosperity-shaped interpretations of mountain-moving faith can become spiritually cruel.
If faith means that believers can guarantee desired outcomes, what do we do with Paul?
Paul prayed repeatedly concerning his “thorn in the flesh.”
Three times he pleaded with the Lord for it to leave him.
Surely Paul knew how to believe.
Surely the apostle who endured beatings, imprisonment, persecution, shipwreck, hunger, and suffering for Christ cannot reasonably be dismissed as someone who simply lacked faith.
Yet the thorn remained.
And Jesus answered him:
“Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου.”
Arkei soi hē charis mou.
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Those words from 2 Corinthians 12:9 expose one of the deepest misunderstandings about faith.
Sometimes faith moves the mountain.
Sometimes faith walks through the valley beneath it.
Sometimes faith watches the Red Sea divide.
Sometimes faith enters the furnace.
Sometimes faith sees prison doors open.
Sometimes faith sings while the doors remain closed.
Sometimes God removes the thorn.
Sometimes Christ says:
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Both can require faith.
This is why Hebrews 11 is so devastatingly beautiful.
We love the first half of the chapter's victories.
Kingdoms conquered.
Promises obtained.
Lions' mouths shut.
The power of fire quenched.
Weakness turned into strength.
Those are the testimonies we put on posters.
But Hebrews does not stop there.
Others were tortured.
Others endured imprisonment.
Others were persecuted.
Others wandered destitute and afflicted.
And Scripture commends them too.
Same chapter.
Same faith.
Different earthly outcomes.
If victorious faith necessarily meant controlling circumstances, Hebrews 11 would contradict itself.
Instead, it reveals something deeper:
Faithfulness to God cannot be measured simply by whether suffering disappeared.
And then we come to Jesus.
Gethsemane.
Night.
Agony.
The cross approaching.
Christ prayed:
“πάτερ μου, εἰ δυνατόν ἐστιν, παρελθάτω ἀπ᾽ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο…”
“Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me…”
And then:
“πλὴν οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω ἀλλ᾽ ὡς σύ.”
“Yet not as I will, but as You will.”
Matthew 26:39.
There may be no clearer destruction of the idea that faith means forcing desired outcomes.
Jesus asked.
Jesus desired.
Jesus submitted.
And submission was not unbelief.
Submission was perfect obedience.
Christ did not fail because the cup remained.
The cross was not evidence that prayer had malfunctioned.
The cross was the road through which redemption came.
Sometimes the thing that looks like unanswered prayer from Friday becomes the evidence of God's victorious wisdom on Sunday.
But Friday still hurts.
And Christianity never asks us to pretend otherwise.
Jesus Himself wept.
Jesus Himself experienced anguish.
Jesus Himself prayed with such intensity in Gethsemane that Luke describes His sweat like drops of blood falling to the ground.
Biblical faith does not require emotional dishonesty.
You can trust God and cry.
You can trust God and ask why.
You can trust God and admit that you desperately want the mountain gone.
You can trust God while your hands shake.
You can say, as the desperate father said to Jesus in Mark 9:24:
“Πιστεύω· βοήθει μου τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ.”
Pisteuō; boēthei mou tē apistia.
“I believe; help my unbelief.”
What an extraordinary confession.
Not polished.
Not impressive.
Not religiously sanitized.
“I believe.”
“Help my unbelief.”
And Jesus did not crush him for admitting the struggle.
Maybe that is the prayer you need tonight.
Not another performance.
Not another declaration designed to convince yourself that you never feel afraid.
Just:
Jesus, I believe.
Help my unbelief.
Because the Gospel was never about you becoming powerful enough to control your life.
It is about being reconciled to the God who holds your life.
Sin taught humanity to grasp for control.
From Eden onward, the temptation has been hauntingly familiar:
You can be like God.
We want sovereignty without surrender.
Power without dependence.
Blessing without obedience.
A crown without a cross.
And religious language can disguise the same ancient temptation.
We can even turn “faith” into another method of trying to become sovereign.
But Jesus does not come merely to improve our techniques for controlling life.
He comes to save sinners.
He comes to reconcile rebels.
He comes to forgive the guilty.
He comes to make dead hearts alive.

He comes to take people imprisoned by sin, shame, pride, fear, lust, bitterness, greed, self-righteousness, addiction, resentment, and secret darkness—and call them into repentance, grace, forgiveness, holiness, and new life.
That is a mountain no human being can move.
You cannot forgive your own sin.
You cannot resurrect your own soul.
You cannot manufacture reconciliation with a holy God.
You cannot scrub yourself clean enough to undo your rebellion.
But Christ went to the cross.
The scandal is that the sinless One was crucified while sinners deserved judgment.
The grace is that He willingly stood where guilty people belonged.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now forgiveness is not purchased by the intensity of your faith.
Salvation rests upon the sufficiency of Christ.
Faith receives.
Christ saves.
Maybe the greatest mountain in your life is not the circumstance you keep begging God to change.
Maybe it is the heart you keep protecting from Him.
Maybe you want Jesus to move your financial mountain while refusing to surrender your greed.
Maybe you want Him to move your relationship mountain while refusing to forgive.
Maybe you want Him to remove consequences while you keep returning to the sin creating them.
Maybe you want breakthrough without repentance.
Maybe you want Jesus as Deliverer while resisting Jesus as Lord.
That is where this message becomes uncomfortable.
Because mountain-moving faith is not permission to command God.
It is an invitation to trust Him so deeply that even your desire for control can be placed on the altar.
Real faith can pray boldly.
Real faith can ask for healing.
Ask.
Real faith can pray for restoration.
Pray.
Real faith can plead for provision, deliverance, reconciliation, open doors, rescued children, transformed marriages, freedom from bondage, and miracles that human beings cannot produce.
Our God is able.
Never shrink Him down to what you can explain.
Never stop praying merely because something looks impossible.
But after pouring your heart before God, biblical faith still knows how to whisper the words our Savior prayed:
“Not my will, but Yours.”
That sentence is not surrender to hopelessness.
It is surrender to God.
And there is an enormous difference.
Faith does not say, “God must do what I have decided.”
Faith says, “God can do what I cannot—and He remains trustworthy even when His wisdom takes me somewhere I would never have chosen.”
That kind of faith terrifies hell more than religious bravado ever could.
Because how do you defeat someone whose confidence is ultimately anchored in Christ rather than circumstances?
Give them abundance—they worship Jesus.
Take away abundance—they worship Jesus.
Open the door—they thank Jesus.
Close the door—they follow Jesus.
Heal them—they glorify Jesus.
Make them wait—they cling to Jesus.
Put them on the mountaintop—they praise Him.
Lead them through the valley of the shadow of death—and somehow, through tears, they still say:
“You are with me.”
That is faith.
Not control.
Trust.
And maybe this article found you while you are standing in front of something that still refuses to move.
I will not insult your pain by promising that reading these words means God will remove it tomorrow.
I cannot promise you the diagnosis will reverse.
I cannot promise the person will return.
I cannot promise the money will appear.
I cannot promise the door will open.
Scripture does not authorize me to make those guarantees.
But I can tell you what Scripture allows us to say with confidence:
God has not ceased being God because you cannot understand what He is doing.
Christ has not stopped being sufficient because you are hurting.
The resurrection has not become less true because Friday has lasted longer than you expected.
And if you belong to Jesus, your final story is not abandonment.
Your final story is resurrection.
Your final story is redemption.
Your final story is Christ.
So pray for the mountain.
Ask God to move it.
Ask boldly.
Ask repeatedly.
Believe that He is able.
But do not worship the outcome.
Worship Jesus.
And if the mountain moves, glorify Him.
If you must climb, depend on Him.
If you must wait, wait with Him.
If the path takes you through suffering, remember that the Savior you follow has scars.
Christianity is not the story of a God shouting instructions safely from the other side of human pain.
God the Son entered our suffering.
Jesus was betrayed.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Buried.
Then resurrection rewrote what looked like defeat.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one truth:
Maybe He is rewriting your understanding of faith right now.
Maybe you spent years believing that stronger faith would finally give you control.
But Christ is offering something better than control.
Communion.
Something better than getting everything you request.
God Himself.
Something better than a life where mountains never appear.
A Savior who will never abandon His people.
So be honest.
Has your faith been resting in Jesus—or in getting the answer you wanted from Jesus?
And when you see someone else write those words, do not treat them like engagement statistics.
Pray for them.
There is a human soul behind that comment.
Someone may be typing through tears.
Someone may be fighting to stay sober.
Someone may be sitting outside an ICU.
Someone may be grieving a marriage.
Someone may be questioning whether God still sees them.
Someone may be one prayer away from finally admitting they cannot carry themselves anymore.
Let the body of Christ act like the body of Christ.
Let your feed become one more place where Scripture, conviction, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and the good news of Jesus Christ can be encountered.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that your faith is genuine. It does not.
Not because God needs our platform.
He does not.

We support Gospel work because everything already belongs to Him, and because voluntarily helping sound Christian teaching reach more people can itself become an act of stewardship and generosity when it is done freely, wisely, and for His glory.
But hear this clearly:
The discount is not the Gospel.
Gospel Warrior is not the Gospel.
Jesus Christ is the center.
If you never buy a product but these words drive you back to Scripture, toward repentance, into prayer, and closer to Jesus, then something far more valuable than a transaction has happened.
If you cannot, you can still help.
Send it privately to someone who is suffering.
Whatever you do, do it for the glory of God—not from guilt, pressure, or the belief that you can purchase His blessing.
Because the Gospel destroys that lie too.
Grace cannot be bought.
Christ already paid the price.
And perhaps that is the final mountain that needs to fall today:
the belief that faith means controlling God.
It doesn't.
Faith means trusting Him.
Even before the answer.
Even after the disappointment.
Even inside the waiting.
Even when your prayers are trembling.
Even when all you can manage is:
“I believe; help my unbelief.”
The mountain may move.
The mountain may remain.
But if your life is anchored in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ, the mountain does not get the final word.
Jesus does.

And sometimes the greatest miracle is not watching God move the mountain in front of you—it is discovering that while you were begging Him to change your circumstances, Christ was transforming the person standing before them.
